cfg = load_config()
s5, s6, s10 = table("phase_05_stats.json"), table("phase_06_stats.json"), table("phase_10_city.json")

year = pd.Timestamp(cfg["study"]["dates"][0]).year

## Pipeline

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(f"""1. **Heights.** The 2022 LiDAR survey gives the height of the ground, every building and every tree at 1 m.
2. **Shadows.** For 24 sun positions ({days}, {year}, every hour from 8:00 to 19:00), we look from a point every 2 m along each
   sidewalk towards the sun. The point is in *building shade* if a building, bridge or the terrain is in the way, in *tree shade*
   if only trees are, and otherwise in the sun. The sun of an hour is placed half an hour before it (the sun of 15:00 at 14:30),
   the moment the heat model uses for the hour's radiation, so shade and heat describe the same moment.
3. **Heat.** The SOLWEIG model turns the same heights into the mean radiant temperature a standing person feels at every square
   metre, from direct sun, the sky, walls and the ground, with the weather of those two days. Together with air temperature,
   humidity and wind this gives the **UTCI**, a thermal-comfort temperature in °C.
4. **Sidewalks.** Each stretch of sidewalk gets, for every hour, its metres of sun, tree shade and building shade, and its UTCI.
5. **Routes.** For every walk we find three routes: the **shortest**, the **shadiest** (lowest shade cost) and the **coolest**
   (lowest heat cost), with the two costs below.""")
```

## The cost of a sunny metre

The shadiest walk uses the cost function of Wen et al. (2025):

$$C = L_{\text{sun}} + (1 - 0.5\,\theta)\,L_{\text{tree}} + (1 - \theta)\,L_{\text{building}} + (1 - 1.5\,\theta)\,L_{\text{indoor}}$$

A metre in the sun costs 1. A metre in tree shade costs a little less (1 − 0.5θ), a metre in building shade less again (1 − θ), and an air-conditioned indoor metre the least (1 − 1.5θ): tree shade sits between sun and building shade. The reward θ grows with the distance already walked, so shade matters more the longer you have been in the heat:

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "θ as a function of distance already walked."
t = cfg["routing"]["theta_curve"]
x = np.linspace(0, 1500, 300)
th = t["a"] / (1 + np.exp(-t["k"] * (x - t["x0"]))) + t["b"]
f, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.plot(x, th, color=C["cool"], lw=2.5)
for d in (300, 800, 1200):
    y = t["a"] / (1 + np.exp(-t["k"] * (d - t["x0"]))) + t["b"]
    ax.scatter([d], [y], color=C["sun"], zorder=3)
    ax.annotate(f"{d} m: θ = {y:.2f}", (d, y), xytext=(6, -14), textcoords="offset points", color=C["dim"], fontsize=9)
ax.set(xlabel="distance already walked (m)", ylabel="θ", ylim=(0, 0.65))
chart(f)
```

Because θ stays near 0.2 for the first 500 m, the shadiest walk on a short trip only leaves the shortest one when that costs almost no extra distance.

## The cost of a hot metre

```{python}
#| output: asis
bh = pd.DataFrame(s10["by_hour"]).set_index("label")
k = [f"{d[5:7]}{d[8:10]}_{cfg['study']['key_hour']:02d}" for d in cfg["study"]["dates"]]
us, ub = bh.loc[k, "u_sun"].mean(), bh.loc[k, "u_bldg"].mean()
print(f"""The coolest walk keeps the same θ, so it is just as willing to detour, but values each metre by its UTCI instead of
its shade class:

$$C_{{\\text{{heat}}}} = \\sum_{{\\text{{edges}}}} L\\,(1 - \\theta\\,r), \\qquad r = \\frac{{U_{{\\text{{sun}}}} - U}}{{U_{{\\text{{sun}}}} - U_{{\\text{{building}}}}}}$$

$U$ is the edge's UTCI; $U_{{\\text{{sun}}}}$ and $U_{{\\text{{building}}}}$ are the median UTCI of all sunlit and all building-shaded sidewalk
points in the city at that hour (at 15:00 about {us:.1f} °C and {ub:.1f} °C). A metre as hot as a typical sunny one costs 1, as the sun
does above, and a metre as cool as typical building shade costs 1 − θ, as building shade does. Everything else follows from its UTCI:
tree shade costs what its measured coolness says, a sunny metre next to hot walls costs more than 1, and an unusually cool
shaded metre less than 1 − θ ($r$ is kept between −1 and 1.5). Indoor passages have no UTCI, so the coolest walk stays outdoors.""")
```

## Metrics

| Metric | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| **Sun** | |
| Sun share | metres in the sun on the shortest walk ÷ its length |
| Sun reduction | (sun on shortest − sun on shadiest) ÷ sun on shortest |
| Weighted exposure reduction | (C of shortest − C of shadiest) ÷ C of shortest |
| No cooler option | the shadiest walk avoids less than 2% of the sun (the break after the spike at 0 in the distribution of 300–1,200 m walks) |
| **Heat** | |
| UTCI of a walk | length-weighted mean UTCI along it, in °C |
| UTCI reduction | UTCI of the shortest walk − UTCI of the coolest (or shadiest) walk, in °C |
| Extreme heat stress | metres with UTCI ≥ 46 °C, the top class of the UTCI scale |
| **Both** | |
| Detour | (length of the walk − shortest length) ÷ shortest length |
| Indoor Contribution Index | (1 − L<sub>shadiest</sub> ÷ L<sub>shortest, outdoor</sub>) × indoor share of the shadiest path's shade (Wen et al. 2025) |

Sun reduction and weighted exposure answer different questions: the first is how much sun you can avoid, the second how much the walk's shade-weighted burden falls when shade is valued at θ. With θ around 0.2, avoiding one metre of sun lowers C by only about 0.15–0.2 m, so weighted exposure falls roughly a tenth as much as sun. UTCI reduction measures the same thing physically, in degrees.

## Indoor scenarios (University City)

Each mapped entrance is linked to the nearest sidewalk, and passages through a building count as indoor, air-conditioned walking. Three cases are compared: outdoor only, adding the buildings open without a Penn ID, and adding all mapped buildings. The shortest route is always the outdoor one. Indoor passages are part of the shade analysis only; they have no UTCI.

## How we checked

The five rapid-transit stations with the largest sun reduction were checked by eye on aerial photos (see Results). The heat model was checked against the shadow model and against itself: see the [technical notes](technical.qmd).
